title: Supplies and Durable Medical Equipment Concepts

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe supplies and durable medical equipment (DME) and how each is classified and billed.
- Relate supplies and DME to HCPCS Level II coding, including code ranges and modifiers.
- Apply medical necessity and documentation requirements to supplies and DME claims.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

HCPCS is a big alphabet of codes that helps offices and insurance companies speak the same language when they talk about supplies and equipment.

### Question 2

Think of HCPCS Level II as the special list of codes for the 'stuff' a patient needs, like a wheelchair or bandages, rather than the doctor's visit itself.

### Question 3

HCPCS Level II codes are like a license plate that always starts with one big letter and then four numbers.

### Question 4

HCPCS has two shelves: Level I holds codes for things doctors do, and Level II holds codes for the supplies and equipment patients need.

### Question 5

The wheelchair is the 'thing,' so it gets a code from the 'things' list (HCPCS Level II), not the 'reason' list or the 'procedure' list.

### Question 6

The diagnosis is the 'why' the patient needs care, and ICD-10-CM is the codebook for all the 'whys.'

### Question 7

CPT is the codebook for what the clinician 'does,' like fixing a cut, while the supply list and the reason list are separate books.

### Question 8

CMS is the 'librarian' in charge of the HCPCS Level II list of supplies and equipment codes.

### Question 9

The 'J' codes are the medicine aisle of the HCPCS store, while 'E' is the equipment aisle and 'L' is the braces-and-artificial-limbs aisle.

### Question 10

The 'E' aisle is for equipment like wheelchairs and hospital beds that a patient uses at home over and over.

### Question 11

S codes are like a special menu some private insurance restaurants use, but the big Medicare restaurant has a different menu and does not serve from it.

### Question 12

Using the same code list is like everyone using the same units of measurement so there is no confusion about what was ordered or billed.

### Question 13

A gauze pad is like a paper towel you use once and throw away, while a wheelchair is like a bicycle you keep using for years.

### Question 14

Durable means 'built to last,' like a sturdy bicycle, not a paper plate you use once.

### Question 15

A walker is 'medical' because you mostly need it after an injury, while a comfy recliner chair is something almost anyone might want.

### Question 16

A commode is like a sturdy chair that gets used many times, while swabs and gauze are like tissues you use once and toss.

### Question 17

The underpad is like a paper plate you throw away, but a walker, wheelchair, and lift are like sturdy tools you keep using.

### Question 18

DME should be like a good backpack that lasts for several school years, not something that wears out in a few weeks.

### Question 19

An oxygen concentrator is like a big machine that keeps working day after day, not a one-time-use item.

### Question 20

A CPAP machine is like a little fan that helps a person breathe all night, every night, for a long time.

### Question 21

A brace or artificial arm attaches to or takes the place of a body part, while a walker is a separate tool the person holds onto.

### Question 22

DMEPOS is a handy abbreviation for the four big groups of things patients might need: equipment, artificial limbs, braces, and supplies.

### Question 23

DME has to be something a patient can safely use where they live, like a walker in their hallway, not a machine that only works in a hospital.

### Question 24

Just wanting something comfortable is like wanting a fancy pillow; it is not the same as needing a medical device for a health condition.

### Question 25

DME is like a reusable water bottle, and supplies are like paper cups you throw away.

### Question 26

Test strips are like sticky notes you use once and throw away, not like a machine you keep for years.

### Question 27

A hospital bed is a big, sturdy piece of equipment a patient uses at home, not something the office uses up like paper.

### Question 28

Medical necessity means the doctor can show a real health reason for the item, not just that the patient wants it.

### Question 29

Deciding if something is medically needed is the doctor's job, like deciding what medicine a patient needs.

### Question 30

The assistant is like a helpful guide who points the question to the doctor instead of answering it themselves.

### Question 31

To prove an item is needed, you show the 'why' (the diagnosis) and the doctor's note saying the item is required.

### Question 32

The diagnosis code is the 'because' that explains the 'what' on the claim, like showing your work in math class.

### Question 33

If something is just 'nice to have' rather than needed for a health problem, insurance usually will not pay for it.

### Question 34

LCDs and NCDs are like rulebooks that tell which equipment Medicare will help pay for and under what conditions.

### Question 35

Before ordering big equipment, the doctor must actually see the patient, like checking that a person really needs a heavy backpack before buying one.

### Question 36

A CMN is like a form that tells the insurance company, 'Here is the health reason this patient needs this equipment.'

### Question 37

The CMN is like a doctor's note for school; only the doctor can write the medical part, even if a helper fills in the name and address.

### Question 38

No proof means no payment, like turning in homework without showing the answers.

### Question 39

KX is like a checkmark that says, 'I have all the proof the rules require,' attached to the claim.

### Question 40

You need the doctor's 'green light' (an order) before equipment can be handed over and billed, like needing a note before borrowing equipment.

### Question 41

A good order is like a complete recipe: it names the item, who it is for, who asked for it, and why.

### Question 42

A signature is like a promise from the doctor saying, 'Yes, I checked this and I approve it on this day.'

### Question 43

If there is a mistake, you tell the teacher (the doctor) and let them fix it the right way instead of erasing it yourself.

### Question 44

Making up information in a medical record is like cheating on a test; it is always wrong and has serious consequences.

### Question 45

Writing down something that did not happen is like telling a lie on an official form; the right move is to tell a trusted supervisor.

### Question 46

Documentation is the 'receipt' that proves the service was real and needed; without it, the money can be taken back.

### Question 47

The assistant is like a checklist helper who makes sure all the required papers are there, not the person who writes the doctor's reasoning.

### Question 48

Keeping the papers is like saving receipts in case someone asks to see them later, even after the purchase is done.

### Question 49

To connect 'why' and 'what,' you need the doctor's order and the notes showing the health reason for it.

### Question 50

Verifying benefits is like checking the map before a trip, so there are no surprises about what insurance will cover.

### Question 51

An ABN is like a heads-up note saying, 'Medicare might not pay for this, so you might have to.'

### Question 52

A modifier is like a small tag added to a code that says 'this one is new' or 'this one is rented.'

### Question 53

NU is like a 'brand new' sticker on the equipment code.

### Question 54

UE is like a 'previously owned' sticker on the equipment code.

### Question 55

RR is like a 'rental' sign, meaning the patient uses it for a while but the supplier still owns it.

### Question 56

Oxygen machines are usually rented month by month, like leasing a car, rather than bought all at once.

### Question 57

Capped rental is like renting a couch until you have paid enough that it becomes yours.

### Question 58

Some things you rent (like oxygen machines) and some things you buy outright (like a simple cane).

### Question 59

The modifier just tells the truth about whether the equipment is fresh out of the box or previously owned.

### Question 60

EY is like a claim admitting, 'There is no doctor's note,' which means the insurance will likely say no.

### Question 61

Competitive bidding is like asking several stores to submit their best price, and Medicare contracts with the winning stores.

### Question 62

To sell equipment to Medicare, a supplier must pass a background check of rules, like getting a special license.

### Question 63

Verifying benefits is like calling ahead to check what is included before ordering, instead of guessing.

### Question 64

The doctor writes the order, the insurance gives the approval, and the bill (claim) asks for the money.

### Question 65

When a bill is turned down, the assistant plays detective to find the missing piece and helps fix it the right way.

### Question 66

The assistant should say, 'It depends on your plan, and I will check for you,' instead of making a promise they cannot keep.

### Question 67

Assignment is like signing a note that says, 'Send the check straight to the store, not to me.'

### Question 68

The 'A' aisle holds bandages, ambulance rides, and other supply-and-transport items.

### Question 69

Cheap, everyday equipment like a simple cane is bought outright, not rented month after month.

### Question 70

The doctor picks the right equipment for the patient's needs, like a coach picking the right gear for a player.

### Question 71

The assistant can hand out brochures, but the 'which one is best' question goes to the doctor, like asking a coach which gear fits best.

### Question 72

Share only the small piece of information the supplier truly needs, like giving one page instead of the whole notebook.

### Question 73

Before sharing private papers, check that there is a real reason and the right permission, like getting a hall pass before leaving class.

### Question 74

If a bill lists something that never happened, the right move is to tell a supervisor, not to pay it or make up a note.

### Question 75

Billing for a fancy bike when the patient got a basic one is cheating the insurance company, and it is against the rules.

### Question 76

The assistant is like a careful data-entry helper who enters what is authorized and raises a hand when something looks off.

### Question 77

If you cannot read the instructions, you ask the person who wrote them instead of making up an answer.

### Question 78

The assistant is the messenger who calls the repair shop, not the mechanic who fixes the machine.

### Question 79

The assistant can look up what the plan covers, but the bigger rent-or-buy choice is a team decision with the doctor.

### Question 80

The assistant handles the paperwork and the follow-up phone calls, while the doctor handles the medical decisions.

### Question 81

If you see something wrong, you tell a trusted adult in charge, not hide it or shout it on the internet.

### Question 82

The equipment has to be safe and usable where the patient actually lives, like in an apartment or house.

### Question 83

Getting prior authorization is like getting permission from the insurance before the big purchase, using the doctor's paperwork.

### Question 84

Big equipment needs more paperwork (like a title for a car), while boxes of supplies need simpler tracking (like a shopping list).

### Question 85

If the 'why' does not match the 'what,' the insurance can take the money back, like returning a purchase that does not match the receipt.
